items.title: Jensen Huang Says He Would Return as Nvidia CEO if Asked
items.author: Kalley Huang
items.content: <article>Mr. Huang resigned as chief executive of the company last week after revelations that he had affairs with an employee and a woman linked to Chinese intelligence.</article>
items.lbText:
Jensen Huang said on Tuesday that he was willing to return to Nvidia as chief executive if its board asked him to do so, in his first public statement since resigning last week.

“I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as C.E.O.,” Mr. Huang said on Tuesday. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as C.E.O.”

Mr. Huang resigned from the company he co-founded after he admitted he was unfaithful to his wife. The New York Times has reported that he had an affair with an employee at Nvidia , as well as a businesswoman who U.S. intelligence has determined is an asset for Chinese intelligence .

Mr. Huang has the backing of a number of allies in Silicon Valley and Wall Street. But Nvidia’s board is not considering reinstating him, according to a person familiar with their thinking who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The board, which includes early investors and business partners who have been close to Mr. Huang for decades, said on Tuesday it had formed a committee to oversee Nvidia’s national security policies, compliance with U.S. trade restrictions and risk management for global trade.

Mr. Huang’s allies started a campaign for his return to Nvidia over the weekend, saying his exit from the company would set the United States back in the artificial intelligence race and blaming Nvidia’s board for bowing to pressure. President Trump also said on Monday that he “would not mind” if Mr. Huang returned to his job and that he thought Mr. Huang had “learned a big lesson.”

items.title: A More Precise Clock Is on Its Way
items.author: Penelope Colston
items.content: <article>The optical atomic clock, which scientists say would be off by about a second over 14 billion years, is soon expected to become a primary reference.</article>
items.lbText:
The world has been undergoing change in everything from the climate to artificial intelligence — and soon time itself is expected to undergo a major transformation.

As early as 2030, the optical atomic clock is expected to become the primary reference for global timekeeping, redefining the second as an element of time and playing a greater role alongside the conventional atomic clocks now used to maintain Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, standards managed by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (generally known by its French abbreviation B.I.P.M.) in Sèvres, France.

These extraordinarily accurate clocks, scientists say, also eventually would assist and replace some of the atomic clocks now used in telecommunications, satellite navigation and other systems that depend on ultraprecise timing for synchronizing cellphone networks; time stamping financial transactions and tracking the movement of airplanes, cars and ships around the world.

In the countdown to the shift, optical atomic clocks are in production at many universities and research institutions as well as a handful of companies — including Rolex, which already has three that it uses to calibrate testing systems and to contribute to the computation of UTC. (According to Rolex’s website, one of the clocks was the first optical atomic clock to take part in the computation of UTC.)

“There are many different types of optical clock and many research groups and start-ups trying to develop or improve them and bring them to market,” Florian Schreck, the coordinator of the AQuRA optical atomic clock consortium, a collaborative project in Europe, said in an email.

While atomic clocks aren’t exactly sluggish — they break a second into about 9 billion parts, which scientists call ticks — their optical counterparts tick hundreds of trillions of times per second and are astoundingly accurate . Researchers say that if an optical atomic clock had started when the universe began, about 14 billion years ago, it would be off by just about one second today.

items.title: Madison Huang, Jensen Huang’s Daughter, Became a Powerful Force at Nvidia
items.author: Kalley Huang, Tripp Mickle and Ryan Mac
items.content: <article>Installed as her father’s de facto chief of staff, Jensen Huang’s daughter alienated top executives. Now her lingering role poses a test for interim C.E.O. Colette Kress.</article>
items.lbText:
Madison Huang was yelling. Her father, Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had been scheduled to headline a conference in New Delhi in February. Shortly before the event, Mr. Huang pulled out and tapped a longtime lieutenant, Jay Puri, to attend in his place.

But Nvidia hadn’t buttoned up its plans for the conference, infuriating Ms. Huang. On a call ahead of the event, Ms. Huang berated other employees — including Mr. Puri — for being unprepared, said three people familiar with the meeting. Eventually, Mr. Puri interrupted and told Ms. Huang he could answer her questions if she stopped yelling at him.

Less than six months later, Mr. Puri left his role at Nvidia.

The tense meeting highlighted the powerful and sometimes disruptive role Ms. Huang, 35, played at the company her father co-founded, according to more than a dozen current and former employees who spoke on condition of anonymity about the family’s leadership of Nvidia. Before Mr. Huang resigned last week, she had become his de facto chief of staff, with considerable authority over more seasoned executives.

That influence creates an immediate challenge for Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive, who replaced Mr. Huang after his resignation last week. Ms. Kress must quickly determine how much power Ms. Huang will have in the company after her father’s exit. She must also decide what to do about Mr. Huang’s other family members employed at the company: his son, Spencer Huang, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez.

Mr. Huang resigned after revelations that he had had extramarital relationships with an Nvidia executive and a customer that U.S. intelligence concluded was working for Chinese intelligence .

The continued presence of Ms. Huang has raised concerns among senior executives that she has conflicted loyalties between the company and her father. Those concerns were heightened over the last few days as Mr. Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street started a campaign to reinstate him, and President Trump said he “ would not mind ” if Mr. Huang returned to his job.

items.title: California Sues OpenAI Over A.I. Safety Issues
items.author: David McCabe
items.content: <article>The state attorney general filed a lawsuit accusing the company of failing to put appropriate safeguards on its artificial intelligence and putting the public at risk.</article>
items.lbText:
California sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the company of putting the public at risk by failing to put appropriate safeguards on its artificial intelligence.

The lawsuit is the latest broadside at the company, which — along with other tech industry players — has faced scrutiny over a rush to develop A.I. at the potential expense of consumer safety.

In a 31-page lawsuit, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, the state said OpenAI’s lax safeguards led to cyberattacks by its A.I. products during testing, including a breach this year when OpenAI’s agents went rogue and attacked the A.I. start-up Hugging Face’s systems . OpenAI’s behavior created a public nuisance and violated a legal prohibition on unfair or fraudulent business practices, the state said.

“OpenAI’s failure to adequately secure and monitor the testing of its highly capable and increasingly powerful A.I. models represents a danger to the public that must be remedied,” the state said in the lawsuit.

The move is the latest effort by a state to rein in the power of A.I. companies in the face of growing concerns about the technology’s ability to go rogue. In recent months, A.I. systems produced by major companies including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have broken out of testing environments designed to keep them from launching cyberattacks on companies and governments, raising alarms.

Courts must still decide how legal liability will be applied in those cases. But there are growing calls for developers of powerful A.I. systems to be held responsible when those systems behave unexpectedly.

items.title: Fan Fiction Site AO3 Returns, and So Do Its Readers, in Droves
items.author: Adeel Hassan
items.content: <article>The archive, which is home to tales inspired by the likes of “Harry Potter” and “Heated Rivalry,” was taken down more than two weeks ago, leaving its fans bereft.</article>
items.lbText:
It’s a library of nearly 19 million works, more than double the circulating materials of the New York Public Library, so when it was knocked offline in a “security incident” more than two weeks ago, its 12 million users were aghast.

The volunteers who run the fan fiction site AO3, short for “ Archive of Our Own ,” had quickly assured its enormous community that no data — especially all those works — had been lost and that it would be restored in four weeks.

But on Sunday, the repository of homespun stories based on works like “Harry Potter,” “Twilight” and “Heated Rivalry” was mostly back online, with some features — like importing external work — temporarily disabled, to help the site return earlier than expected.

“The intensity of the response speaks to how deeply fan fiction has become woven into our lives,” Dana Bryce , a writer and cultural commentator in Toronto, said on Sunday afternoon.

“The AO3 outage has shown how deeply participatory storytelling is now embedded in everyday cultural life,” Ms. Bryce said. “And its absence made the importance of that relationship visible.”

The works hosted on the nonprofit, noncommercial archive are inspired by books, films and even celebrities, like the members of K-pop bands. It is run entirely by volunteers, and operated by the Organization for Transformative Works.

“Modern audiences are voracious,” Ms. Bryce said. “We want more, always. And nowhere is that more true than in stories. We are increasingly dissatisfied with the finality of the close of novels, television series and films. Stories have become worlds that audiences want to revisit indefinitely.”

She said that fan fiction democratizes storytelling, and that AO3 readers were not limited by long publishing cycles or a single author’s pen.

“It’s a shared experience,” she said. “Instead of reading in silos, audiences can read and write as a collective, reimagining, revising, reinterpreting and expanding fictional worlds, becoming active participants in storytelling.”

AO3 said on Sunday that it would not disclose what had happened to the site, referring to the outage as a “security incident.”

It said it would not share specifics of mitigating changes it was putting in place but did say it was consulting with a security firm.

It recommended that users change their passwords, while noting that “we have no reason to believe that the user database was compromised.”

There was so much site traffic on Sunday that some users faced delays loading it. “This is an intentional measure to help manage traffic,” AO3 said.

Ms. Bryce was not surprised by readers’ response on Sunday, calling AO3 “a collective cultural archive.”

“It’s a living record of evolving audience desires and attachments,” she said.

Adeel Hassan, a New York-based reporter for The Times, covers breaking news and other topics.

items.title: The Jensen Huang Scandal Has Shocked Even Scandal-Prone Silicon Valley
items.author: David Streitfeld
items.content: <article>As Jensen Huang abruptly departs, the tech community grapples with an eternal question: Why do the smartest and most successful men so often act so stupidly?</article>
items.lbText:
Artificial intelligence promises transcendence. We will ditch our tired and inefficient bodies, say farewell to tedious work and trips to the grocery store. The computer will tend to all human needs and solve all human problems.

Well, that was the idea. A.I. was supposed to achieve a new level of reality this month with the public sale of shares of Anthropic, one of the two start-ups that have created and defined this young industry. A trillion-dollar company will be born, yielding billionaires galore.

A.I. is the biggest Silicon Valley story ever. But last Sunday it was suddenly pushed aside when the chief executive of the company whose chips are literally powering this intelligence revolution confessed to cheating on his wife with a woman, Alice Huang, who U.S. officials believe was spying for China. By Thursday morning he had resigned, something few thought possible just days earlier.

The scandal that took down Nvidia chief Jensen Huang is full of implications for national security and the global A.I. boom. Mr. Huang ranked among Mark Zuckerberg, Steve Jobs, Elon Musk and Bill Gates as tech leaders who were considered by the world to be inseparable from the companies they built.

In Silicon Valley, people were mostly just stunned by the news. Those who have been around for a long time, and seen the stretch of territory south of San Francisco evolve from hardware manufacturing to software development to the dot-com frenzy and now the A.I. boom, said they had never seen anything like it.

Tech veterans have witnessed amazing ascensions and equally abrupt falls. They have seen abundant arrogance. Fortunes made and fortunes lost in an instant. But there’s something that stands out this time: Transcendence was never supposed to be tawdry.

items.title: How Jensen Huang’s Secret Led to His Downfall at Nvidia
items.author: Tripp Mickle, Ana Swanson, Paul Mozur, Jonathan Swan, Julian E. Barnes and Maggie Haberman
items.content: <article>Nvidia’s leader said his relationship with a female customer was just about business. But what he was concealing eventually led to his resignation from the company he created.</article>
items.lbText:
It was September 2025, and The New York Times had just called his company about a Singaporean data center firm called Megaspeed that had been led by a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, or Huang Le. The Times was reporting that Mr. Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, had a close relationship with her.

Mr. Huang, who Nvidia employees say could have a volcanic temper, wanted to know what The Times was insinuating. Though he didn’t deny that he knew the woman, he was bothered by the suggestion that they might be close, people familiar with the discussion said.

Nvidia mounted an aggressive defense. Madison Huang, Mr. Huang’s daughter who acted as her father’s chief of staff, pressed the company’s communications team to push back forcefully. They also had reinforcements, a crisis communications firm called Heller.

They insisted that Mr. Huang and the woman from Megaspeed just had a business relationship.

Over the next 13 months, Mr. Huang stuck with his story, even after The Times reported last month that the U.S. had gathered intelligence showing that Ms. Huang was secretly working with China’s top spy agency.

But last weekend, facing new revelations about the relationship, Mr. Huang finally came clean to Nvidia’s general counsel. He had been having an affair with the woman, after all, said the people familiar with the discussions.

The relationship with the Megaspeed executive wasn’t Mr. Huang’s only secret.

On Wednesday, a Times reporter called Mr. Huang to ask him about a second extramarital relationship. This time, it was an affair with an executive who reported to him.

items.title: Tech Leaders Rally Behind Jensen Huang
items.author: Kalley Huang
items.content: <article>In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia.</article>
items.lbText:
Many of Silicon Valley’s executives and investors are rallying behind Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday after revelations that he had affairs with an employee and with a woman who U.S. officials believed to be a spy for China .

In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board of directors, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia. Mr. Huang’s exit, they argued, would set the United States back in the artificial intelligence race. And they blamed Nvidia’s board for bowing to pressure.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive and the richest person in the world, said in a social media post on Saturday. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

The support put a spotlight on Nvidia’s role as the linchpin of the A.I. boom and on Mr. Huang’s leadership as the company grew into one of the most valuable in the world. Nvidia, which started making computer chips for video games, now controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy. Along the way, Mr. Huang became Silicon Valley’s consummate dealmaker , turning Nvidia into a central banker for start-ups that needed chips and funding.

“We believe the board should avoid a rush to replace Jensen that undermines and thwarts the best interests of shareholders,” Brad Gerstner, the chief executive of Altimeter Capital Management, and Gavin Baker, the chief investment officer of Atreides Management, wrote in a letter sent on Friday. The investors, whose firms are Nvidia shareholders, asked the company’s board to consider “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”

An open letter to Nvidia’s board , titled “Stand With Jensen,” asked the board to reinstall Mr. Huang as chief executive, to conduct an independent investigation and to explain its actions. As of Saturday morning, the letter had nearly 100,000 signatures, including by current and former employees of Nvidia, business partners like Mr. Musk and start-up leaders and shareholders including Garry Tan, the chief executive of the venture capital firm Y Combinator.
